title: Homeostasis: Temperature, Glucose and Water Balance
standard_text: The stimulus–response model and negative feedback; thermoregulation in endotherms and ectotherms; the nervous and endocrine systems; blood glucose regulation by insulin and glucagon; water balance, ADH and the kidney; plant responses and hormones. (Senior Secondary Biology, Unit 4: Maintaining the internal environment)
meta_desc: Free Year 12 Biology worksheets on homeostasis: negative feedback, thermoregulation, nerves and hormones, insulin and glucagon, ADH, the kidney and plant hormones. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Stimulus → receptor → control centre → effector → response.
key_sub: Negative feedback brings a variable back to its set point.
body_html:
How to think about it

Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable. A change (stimulus) is detected by receptors; a control centre (often the hypothalamus) sends signals by nerves or hormones to effectors, which reverse the change: negative feedback.

Body temperature is controlled by sweating, shivering and changes to skin blood flow. Insulin lowers and glucagon raises blood glucose. ADH controls how much water the kidneys reabsorb. Australian animals such as red kangaroos and hopping mice show special adaptations.

Example

Blood glucose rises after a meal. Which hormone and gland?

detected by the pancreas

beta cells release insulin

Answer: insulin from the pancreas

Example

Filtrate 125 mL/min, urine 1 mL/min. % reabsorbed?

(125 − 1) ÷ 125 × 100

Answer: 99.2%

Common mistakes

  • Saying negative feedback is bad: it is stabilising.
  • Mixing up glucagon (hormone) with glycogen (store).
  • Thinking ADH makes more urine: it makes less, more concentrated urine.

faq.q: How do ectotherms control their temperature?
